metadata.title: A multilevel investigation into teacher-supported student use of technology in East Asian classroom: Examining teacher and school characteristics

survey_design.weight_variable_name: TCHWGT and SCHWGT (teacher within-level and school between-level weights); participating teacher weight product of WGTFAC1 x WGTADJ1 x WGTFAC2 x WGTADJ2 x WGTADJ3 x WGTADJ4; school weight product of WGTFAC1 x WGTADJ1
survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 teacher and principal data from five East Asian economies (CSH, TWN, KOR, JPN, SGP) with a stratified two-stage probability sampling design (schools selected first, then ~20 teachers per school). Analyses are conducted with multilevel structural equation modeling (MSEM) and incorporate complex-sampling weights at both levels: teacher within-level weights (TCHWGT) and school between-level weights (SCHWGT). The participating teacher weight is computed as the product of multiple TALIS weight factors (WGTFAC1, WGTADJ1, WGTFAC2, WGTADJ2, WGTADJ3, WGTADJ4), while the school weight is computed as WGTFAC1 x WGTADJ1, following OECD guidance. The manuscript does not indicate any omission of weights; instead, it explicitly states that these level-specific weights are included in all data analyses to represent the population structure and hierarchical sampling.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TALIS 2018 teacher and principal datasets for five East Asian economies that participated in TALIS 2018 (Chinese Shanghai, Chinese Taipei, Korea, Japan, Singapore). The analytic sample comprises teachers at ISCED level 2 (secondary) within the participating schools, with outcomes defined from two specific TALIS teacher questionnaire items (TSSUT1 and TSSUT2). The study does not report additional task/module restrictions beyond using the TALIS teacher/principal datasets and the specified outcome items; it instead addresses missingness via full-information maximum likelihood (FIML) under the complex sampling design. No further exclusions (e.g., by teacher gender/experience) are described in the provided text.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (teachers, ISCED level 2) — Teacher-supported student use of information technology (TSSUT1)
main_findings.target_variable: Teacher-supported student use of information technology (TSSUT1)
main_findings.performance_metrics: MSEM (full sample): T3SEENG β=0.150 (p<0.001) at teacher level; T3COLES β=0.111 (p<0.001) at teacher level; T3WLOAD β=0.078 (p<0.001) at teacher level. School level (full sample): T3PLACMA β=−0.201 (p=0.004) and T3PAUTI β=0.125 (p=0.083) (others non-significant). Explained variance (R2): teacher level 0.049; school level 0.324 (full sample).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (teachers, ISCED level 2) the study leveraged self-efficacy in student engagement, professional collaboration in lessons, workload stress, lack of material resources, and perceived disciplinary climate to model teacher-supported student use of information technology (TSSUT1), finding that teacher self-efficacy and collaboration were consistently positive while lack of material resources was negatively associated at the school level. This indicates that strengthening teachers’ engagement self-efficacy and collaborative professional practices, alongside improving schools’ material resource capacity, may increase how often teachers allow students to use ICT for learning, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (teachers, ISCED level 2) — Teacher-supported student use of digital technology (TSSUT2)
main_findings.target_variable: Teacher-supported student use of digital technology (TSSUT2)
main_findings.performance_metrics: MSEM (full sample): T3SEENG β=0.285 (p<0.001) at teacher level; T3COLES β=0.037 (p=0.013) at teacher level; T3WLOAD β=0.063 (p=0.001) at teacher level. School level (full sample): T3PLACMA β=−0.163 (p=0.010) and NENRSTUD β=0.212 (p=0.003) were significant; other school-level predictors non-significant. Contextual effects (full sample): T3TEAM β=0.281 (p=0.007) and T3SEENG β=0.172 (p=0.042) predicting TSSUT2. Explained variance (R2): teacher level 0.090; school level 0.267 (full sample).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (teachers, ISCED level 2) the study leveraged self-efficacy in student engagement, professional collaboration in lessons, team innovativeness, workload stress, and lack of material resources to model teacher-supported student use of digital technology (TSSUT2), finding that teacher self-efficacy was the strongest positive predictor and that lack of material resources was negatively associated at the school level. This indicates that policies should prioritize building teachers’ confidence to engage students and fostering collaborative/innovative school climates, while also addressing resource constraints that can suppress digital technology support in classrooms, though causality cannot be inferred from cross-sectional TALIS data.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher and principal data from five East Asian economies (Chinese Shanghai, Chinese Taipei, Singapore, Korea, Japan) to explain teacher-supported student use of technology in secondary schools (ISCED level 2). Two teacher-reported Likert outcomes were used: TSSUT1 (ICT for projects/class work) and TSSUT2 (supporting learning through digital technology). The authors estimate two-level structural equation models with robust maximum-likelihood estimation, incorporating TALIS complex-sampling weights at the teacher (TCHWGT) and school (SCHWGT) levels, and handling missingness via full-information maximum likelihood. Across the full sample, teacher self-efficacy in student engagement was the most consistent positive predictor for both outcomes (TSSUT1 β=0.150, p<0.001; TSSUT2 β=0.285, p<0.001), while lack of material resources was significantly negative at the school level (TSSUT1 β=−0.201, p=0.004; TSSUT2 β=−0.163, p=0.010). The explained variance was modest-to-moderate (e.g., school-level R2=0.324 for TSSUT1 and 0.267 for TSSUT2), and the cross-sectional design plus mono-source teacher reporting limit causal interpretation.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The manuscript is an MSEM-based multilevel analysis of associations (not an ML predictive modeling study), and it does not train or evaluate any machine-learning algorithms. Therefore, ml_techniques.all_techniques is empty and no ML primary model can be identified. The outcomes are modeled using structural equation modeling with robust maximum-likelihood estimation and complex survey weights, so the extraction focuses on multilevel statistical associations rather than ML performance metrics.
